policy_name: Counseling for Career Choice Act
question: According to the Counseling for Career Choice Act, how will schools leverage resources and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to support career development and counseling?
answer_1: The Counseling for Career Choice Act, as amended to the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, includes a provision that schools should leverage resources and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to support career development and counseling. This is specified in Section 4107(a)(3)(A)(x) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, as amended by H.R. 7395. (20 U.S.C. 7117(a)(3)(A))
answer_2: Schools will leverage resources and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to support career development and counseling by implementing a process and infrastructure for school counselors and school counseling programs to access information regarding regional workforce trends, developing and implementing professional development or career development training certification programs for counselors, and evaluating secondary and postsecondary outcomes for individuals served by school or other career counseling programs (H. R. 7395, Section 2, Section 4107(a)(3)(A)(x)).

policy_name: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
question: Summarize the core obligations that organizations are undertaking with respect to frontier AI safety according to the document.
answer_1:
The core obligations that organizations are undertaking with respect to frontier AI safety, according to the document, are as follows:

1. Effective Risk Identification, Assessment, and Management (Outcome 1): Organizations are expected to assess risks across the AI lifecycle, set thresholds for severe risks, articulate risk mitigations, and follow processes if risks exceed thresholds (I-IV). They should also continually invest in advancing their ability to implement these commitments (V).

2. Accountability for Safe Development and Deployment (Outcome 2): Organizations are required to adhere to the commitments outlined in Outcome 1, develop and review internal accountability and governance frameworks, and assign roles, responsibilities, and sufficient resources (VI).

3. Transparency (Outcome 3): Organizations are expected to provide public transparency on the implementation of the commitments, except in cases where doing so would increase risk or divulge sensitive commercial information (VII). They should also explain how external actors are involved in the process of assessing risks and adherence to the safety framework (VIII).

These obligations apply to highly capable general-purpose AI models or systems that can perform a wide variety of tasks and match or exceed the capabilities present in the most advanced models (Frontier AI). The home governments of these organizations are also involved in the process, particularly in defining thresholds and providing input on severe risks (II).

References:
- Frontier AI Safety Commitments: <https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Frontier-AI-Safety-Commitments-1.pdf>
- Definition of 'frontier AI': In the document, the definition of 'frontier AI' is provided in the last paragraph.
- Definition of "home governments": In the document, the definition of "home governments" is provided in the last paragraph.
- Thresholds definition: In the document, thresholds can be defined using model capabilities, estimates of risk, implemented safeguards, deployment contexts, and/or other relevant risk factors (II). It should be possible to assess whether thresholds have been breached (V).
answer_2: 1. Organizations will effectively identify, assess, and manage risks when developing and deploying their frontier AI models and systems (Outcome 1). This includes assessing risks across the AI lifecycle, setting thresholds for intolerable risks, implementing risk mitigations, and continually investing in advancing their ability to implement these commitments. 2. Organizations will be accountable for safely developing and deploying their frontier AI models and systems (Outcome 2). This includes adhering to the commitments outlined in Outcome 1 and continuously reviewing internal accountability and governance frameworks. 3. Organizations will provide appropriate transparency to external actors, including governments, on the implementation of these commitments (Outcome 3). This includes providing public transparency on the implementation of the commitments, except in cases where doing so would increase risk or divulge sensitive commercial information.

policy_name: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
question: Explain how the document defines 'frontier AI' and why this definition is significant for the scope of the commitments.
answer_1: The document defines 'frontier AI' as highly capable general-purpose AI models or systems that can perform a wide variety of tasks and match or exceed the capabilities present in the most advanced models (paragraph 11). This definition is significant for the scope of the commitments because it specifies the type of AI systems that the organizations have agreed to develop and deploy responsibly, focusing on advanced and powerful AI models that have the potential to pose significant risks if not managed properly. By limiting the scope to frontier AI, the commitments aim to address the most pressing safety concerns associated with the most advanced AI systems, rather than less capable AI systems that may pose fewer risks. (Source: AI Safety Commitments, Frontier AI, paragraph 11)
answer_2: The document defines 'frontier AI' as highly capable general-purpose AI models or systems that can perform a wide variety of tasks and match or exceed the capabilities present in the most advanced models (VII). This definition is significant for the scope of the commitments as it specifies the type of AI systems the participating organizations are committing to develop and deploy responsibly, focusing on advanced and powerful AI models.

policy_name: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
question: Describe the three main outcomes the signatory organizations are aiming to achieve and provide an example of a commitment that contributes to each outcome.
answer_1:
1. Outcome 1: Organisations effectively identify, assess, and manage risks when developing and deploying their frontier AI models and systems.
   - Example of a commitment: Organisations will assess the risks posed by their frontier models or systems across the AI lifecycle, including before deploying that model or system, and, as appropriate, before and during training (Commitment I).

2. Outcome 2: Organisations are accountable for safely developing and deploying their frontier AI models and systems.
   - Example of a commitment: Organisations will adhere to the commitments outlined in I-V, including by developing and continuously reviewing internal accountability and governance frameworks and assigning roles, responsibilities, and sufficient resources to do so (Commitment VI).

3. Outcome 3: Organisations’ approaches to frontier AI safety are appropriately transparent to external actors, including governments.
   - Example of a commitment: Organisations will provide public transparency on the implementation of the above (I-VI), except insofar as doing so would increase risk or divulge sensitive commercial information to a degree disproportionate to the societal benefit (Commitment VII).
answer_2: 1. The first outcome is for organizations to effectively identify, assess, and manage risks when developing and deploying their frontier AI models and systems (Outcome 1). An example commitment is setting out thresholds at which severe risks posed by a model or system, unless adequately mitigated, would be deemed intolerable (commitment II). 2. The second outcome is for organizations to be accountable for safely developing and deploying their frontier AI models and systems (Outcome 2). An example commitment is adhering to the commitments outlined in I-V, including by developing and continuously reviewing internal accountability and governance frameworks (commitment VI). 3. The third outcome is for organizations' approaches to frontier AI safety to be appropriately transparent to external actors, including governments (Outcome 3). An example commitment is providing public transparency on the implementation of the above (I-VI), except insofar as doing so would increase risk or divulge sensitive commercial information to a degree disproportionate to the societal benefit (commitment VII).

policy_name: FY2025 NDAA, Section 1514 ("Management and cybersecurity of multi-cloud environments")
question: What are the core components that the Department of Defense's multi-cloud management and cybersecurity strategy, as mandated by Section 1514, must encompass?
answer_1:
1. Alignment with the Department of Defense's zero trust strategy (b(1)).
2. Provision of network visibility and interoperability across the multi-cloud environments (b(2)).
3. Rationalization of user identities across multi-cloud environments, including through the implementation of identity, credential, and access management technologies (b(3)).
4. Maintenance of the same means to secure endpoints across the Department (b(4)).
5. Improvement of the identification and resolution of security concerns for each cloud environment (b(5)).
6. Assessment of means to increase the adoption of artificial intelligence applications into the multi-cloud environments (b(6)).
7. Increase in the transparency of reporting on the usage of multi-cloud environments (b(7)).
8. Identification of opportunities to improve the planning of data use and storage in such cloud environments, including policies and processes to enforce protection of government data (b(8)).
9. Identification of opportunities to streamline certification processes related to the provision of cloud services for cloud service providers (b(9)).
10. A plan for training the necessary personnel on the use and cybersecurity of multi-cloud environments (b(10)).

Citation: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, Section 1514.
answer_2: 1) Align with the DoD Zero Trust Strategy; 2) Provide network visibility and interoperability; 3) Rationalize user identities; 4) Maintain endpoint security; 5) Improve security concern identification and resolution; 6) Assess AI adoption; 7) Increase transparency of reporting; 8) Improve data use and storage planning; 9) Streamline certification processes; 10) Include a plan for personnel training. [Reference: SEC. 1514 (a)(b)(1-10)]

policy_name: FY2025 NDAA, Section 1514 ("Management and cybersecurity of multi-cloud environments")
question: Beyond alignment with the DoD's Zero Trust Strategy, what specific actions will the mandated strategy take to improve the Department's overall cybersecurity posture within its multi-cloud environments?
answer_1:
1. Network visibility and interoperability across the entirety of the multi-cloud environments of the Department (b(2)). This action aims to ensure that the Department has a unified view of its multi-cloud environments, enabling better monitoring and response to potential security threats.

2. Rationalization of user identities across such multi-cloud environments, including through the implementation of identity, credential, and access management technologies (b(3)). This action aims to simplify user access management, reducing the risk of unauthorized access and improving accountability.

3. Maintaining the same means to secure endpoints across the Department (b(4)). This action ensures consistent security measures across all endpoints, reducing the attack surface and improving the Department's ability to respond to threats.

4. Improving the identification and resolution of security concerns for each cloud environment prior to and during the adoption of such cloud environment by the Department (b(5)). This action aims to proactively address security issues, reducing the risk of breaches and improving the Department's overall security posture.

5. Assessing means to increase the adoption of artificial intelligence applications into the multi-cloud environments of the Department (b(6)). While not explicitly stated, the implication is that AI will be used to enhance security, such as through threat detection and response.

6. Increasing the transparency of the reporting by the Department on the usage of such multi-cloud environments by the Department (b(7)). This action aims to improve planning, budgeting, and predictability for users and contractors, potentially reducing inefficiencies and costs.

7. Identifying opportunities to improve the planning of the Department for data use and storage in such cloud environments, including policies and processes to enforce protection of data provided by the Government (b(8)). This action aims to ensure that sensitive data is protected when used for training AI models or other software systems.

8. Identifying opportunities to streamline certification processes related to the provision of cloud services for cloud service providers (b(9)). This action aims to reduce the administrative burden on cloud service providers, potentially leading to lower costs and increased competition.

9. Including a plan for training the necessary personnel of the Department on how to incorporate the use of multi-cloud environments into the performance of the functions of the Department and effectively leverage cybersecurity capabilities in such multi-cloud environments (b(10)). This action
answer_2: 1) The strategy will provide network visibility and interoperability across all multi-cloud environments of the Department (b(2)). 2) It will rationalize user identities, including through the implementation of identity, credential, and access management technologies (b(3)). 3) The strategy will maintain the same means to secure endpoints across the Department (b(4)). 4) It will provide means for improving the identification and resolution of security concerns for each cloud environment (b(5)). 5) It will assess means to increase the adoption of artificial intelligence applications into the multi-cloud environments of the Department (b(6)). 6) It will increase the transparency of reporting on the usage of multi-cloud environments to improve planning, budgeting, and predictability (b(7)). 7) It will identify opportunities to improve data use and storage planning, including policies to enforce protection of government data (b(8)). 8) It will include a plan for training personnel on incorporating multi-cloud environments and leveraging cybersecurity capabilities (c(10)).

policy_name: FY2025 NDAA, Section 1514 ("Management and cybersecurity of multi-cloud environments")
question: How does Section 1514 aim to balance the need for increased adoption of AI applications within the DoD's multi-cloud environments with the imperative to protect government data used in training those AI models?
answer_1:
Section 1514 aims to balance the need for increased adoption of AI applications within the DoD's multi-cloud environments with the imperative to protect government data used in training those AI models by requiring the strategy to identify opportunities to improve the planning of the Department for data use and storage in such cloud environments, including policies and processes to enforce protection of data provided by the Government when such data is used to train artificial intelligence models or other commercially developed software systems (Section 1514(b)(8)). This section does not specify the exact policies or processes to be implemented, but it emphasizes the importance of data protection in the context of AI model training.

Citation: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, H.R. 4350, Sec. 1514.
answer_2: Section 1514 aims to balance the need for increased AI adoption within the DoD's multi-cloud environments with the protection of government data used in training those AI models by requiring the strategy to assess means to increase AI adoption (Sec. 1514(b)(6)) and identify opportunities to enforce protection of data provided by the Government when used to train AI models or other software systems (Sec. 1514(b)(8)).

policy_name: FY2025 NDAA, Section 1514 ("Management and cybersecurity of multi-cloud environments")
question: In what ways does Section 1514 seek to enhance transparency and accountability in the DoD's management and utilization of multi-cloud environments, particularly concerning capacity planning, budgeting, and predictability for users and contractors?
answer_1:
Section 1514 seeks to enhance transparency and accountability in the DoD's management and utilization of multi-cloud environments by requiring the strategy to provide means for improving the reporting by the Department on the usage of such multi-cloud environments (Section 1514(b)(7)). This reporting is intended to improve planning for capacity demand, budgeting, and predictability for users and the contractors of the Department providing such multi-cloud environments and the goods and services related to such multi-cloud environments.

Citation: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, Section 1514.
answer_2: Section 1514 seeks to enhance transparency and accountability in the DoD's management and utilization of multi-cloud environments by requiring the strategy to increase the transparency of reporting on the usage of such multi-cloud environments by the Department (Sec. 1514(b)(7)). This improved reporting aims to help with capacity demand planning, budgeting, and predictability for users and contractors providing these multi-cloud environments and related goods and services.

policy_name: NYC Local Law 144
question: What are the key compliance requirements that employers and employment agencies must meet when using automated employment decision tools under this law?
answer_1:
1. Employers and employment agencies must ensure that their automated employment decision tools have undergone a bias audit conducted no more than one year prior to use (§ 20-871a1).
2. The results of the most recent bias audit and the distribution date of the tool to which the audit applies must be made publicly available on the employer or employment agency's website prior to the use of the tool (§ 20-871a1).
3. Employers and employment agencies must notify candidates or employees who reside in the city that an automated employment decision tool will be used in connection with the assessment or evaluation of such individuals, at least ten business days before such use (§ 20-871b1).
4. Employers and employment agencies must provide candidates or employees with information about the job qualifications and characteristics that the automated employment decision tool will use in the assessment (§ 20-871b2).
5. Upon written request by a candidate or employee, employers and employment agencies must disclose information about the type of data collected for the automated employment decision tool, the source of such data, and the employer or employment agency's data retention policy (§ 20-871b3).
6. Employers and employment agencies may be subject to civil penalties for violations of the provisions of this subchapter (§ 20-872).
7. The provisions of this subchapter do not limit any right of a candidate or employee to bring a civil action in court or the authority of the Commission on Human Rights to enforce the provisions of Title 8 (§ 20-874).

Source: Int. No. 1894-A, Administrative Code of the City of New York, Chapter 5, Subchapter 25.
answer_2: 1. Employers and employment agencies must ensure that the automated employment decision tools they use have undergone a bias audit conducted no more than one year prior to use. 2. A summary of the results of the most recent bias audit and the distribution date of the tool to which the audit applies must be made publicly available on the employer or employment agency's website before the tool is used. 3. Employers and employment agencies must notify candidates or employees who reside in the city that an automated employment decision tool will be used, the job qualifications and characteristics the tool will use, and provide information about the type of data collected, the source of such data, and the employer or employment agency's data retention policy upon written request. These notices must be provided at least 10 business days before the use of the tool. (Section 20-871, Int. No. 1894-A)

policy_name: NYC Local Law 144
question: Describe the process by which candidates or employees residing in NYC will be informed about the use of automated employment decision tools in their assessment, as specified by this law.
answer_1:
1. Candidates or employees residing in NYC will be notified that an automated employment decision tool will be used in connection with the assessment or evaluation of their application or employment, at least ten business days before such use. This notice is required by section 20-871(b)(1) of the administrative code of the city of New York.

2. The job qualifications and characteristics that the automated employment decision tool will use in the assessment of the candidate or employee must also be disclosed, again at least ten business days before such use, as required by section 20-871(b)(2) of the administrative code.

3. If not disclosed on the employer or employment agency’s website, information about the type of data collected for the automated employment decision tool, the source of such data, and the employer or employment agency’s data retention policy shall be available upon written request by a candidate or employee. Such information shall be provided within 30 days of the written request, as required by section 20-871(b)(3) of the administrative code.

4. It is important to note that the law also requires that the summary of the results of the most recent bias audit of the automated employment decision tool, as well as the distribution date of the tool to which such audit applies, has been made publicly available on the website of the employer or employment agency prior to the use of such tool, as required by section 20-871(a) of the administrative code.

Citations: Int. No. 1894-A, § 20-871(b)(1-3), § 20-871(a)
answer_2: 1. Employers or employment agencies using automated employment decision tools must notify candidates or employees residing in NYC about the use of such tools at least 10 business days before their use. 2. The notice must include information about the job qualifications and characteristics used by the tool, as well as the type of data collected, its source, and the employer or agency's data retention policy. 3. If not disclosed on the employer or employment agency's website, this information can be requested in writing and must be provided within 30 days. 4. Candidates or employees can request an alternative selection process or accommodation upon receiving the notice. (Section 20-871(b) of Int. No. 1894-A)

policy_name: NYC Local Law 144
question: What specific elements are required to be included in a bias audit of an automated employment decision tool, as defined within this legislation?
answer_1: A bias audit, as defined within this legislation (Int. No. 1894-A), must include an impartial evaluation by an independent auditor. The audit shall assess the automated employment decision tool's disparate impact on persons of any component 1 category required to be reported by employers pursuant to subsection (c) of section 2000e-8 of title 42 of the United States code as specified in part 1602.7 of title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations. (Section 20-870 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York)
answer_2: A bias audit, as defined in this legislation (Int. No. 1894-A), should include an impartial evaluation by an independent auditor to assess the automated employment decision tool's disparate impact on individuals belonging to any component 1 category required to be reported by employers pursuant to subsection (c) of section 2000e-8 of title 42 of the United States code as specified in part 1602.7 of title 29 of the code of federal regulations.

policy_name: NYC Local Law 144
question: How does this law define 'automated employment decision tool,' and what types of tools are explicitly excluded from this definition?
answer_1: The law defines 'automated employment decision tool' as any computational process, derived from machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics, or artificial intelligence, that issues simplified output, including a score, classification, or recommendation, that is used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decision making for making employment decisions that impact natural persons. The law explicitly excludes a tool that does not automate, support, substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making processes and that does not materially impact natural persons, such as a junk email filter, firewall, antivirus software, calculator, spreadsheet, database, data set, or other compilation of data (Int. No. 1894-A, § 20-870).
answer_2: According to Int. No. 1894-A, an 'automated employment decision tool' is defined as any computational process, derived from machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics, or artificial intelligence, that issues simplified output, including a score, classification, or recommendation, that is used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decision making for making employment decisions that impact natural persons. The term does not include a tool that does not automate, support, substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making processes and that does not materially impact natural persons, such as a junk email filter, firewall, antivirus software, calculator, spreadsheet, database, data set, or other compilation of data.

policy_name: NYC Local Law 144
question: Outline the penalties for violating the provisions of this law, including the range of civil penalties and how repeat violations are addressed.
answer_1:
1. Violations of the provisions of this law or any rules promulgated pursuant to it are subject to a civil penalty.
2. The civil penalty for a first violation is not more than $500, and each additional violation occurring on the same day as the first violation is also subject to a penalty not less than $500 nor more than $1,500.
3. Each day on which an automated employment decision tool is used in violation of the law constitutes a separate violation, resulting in a separate civil penalty.
4. Failure to provide any notice to a candidate or an employee in violation of the law's requirements for notice constitutes a separate violation.
5. A proceeding to recover any civil penalty authorized by this law is returnable to any tribunal established within the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings or within any agency of the city designated to conduct such proceedings.

Citation: Int. No. 1894-A, § 20-872 (a-d) (New York City Council, 2021)
answer_2: 1. A civil penalty of not more than $500 for a first violation and each additional violation occurring on the same day as the first violation. 2. Not less than $500 nor more than $1,500 for each subsequent violation. 3. Each day on which an automated employment decision tool is used in violation of the law shall give rise to a separate violation.

policy_name: Massachusetts AI in Mental Health Act
question: Explain the process a licensed mental health professional must undertake to legally utilize AI in their practice under this act.
answer_1:
1. A licensed mental health professional who wishes to provide mental health services through the use of AI must first seek approval from the relevant professional licensing board (Section 3a).
2. The AI system used to provide mental health services must be designed to prioritize the safety and well-being of individuals seeking treatment and must be continuously monitored by a licensed mental health professional to ensure its safety and effectiveness (Section 3b).
3. The licensed mental health professional must inform patients of the use of AI in their treatment and provide them with the option to receive treatment from a licensed mental health professional (Section 3c).
4. The licensed mental health professional must disclose the use of AI to patients in advance and obtain their informed consent (Section 3d).

Citation: Chapter 123 of the General Laws, as appearing in the 2020 Official Edition, Section 1-4.
answer_2: 1. A licensed mental health professional wishing to use AI in their practice must first seek approval from the relevant professional licensing board (Section 3a). 2. The AI system used must be designed to prioritize the safety and well-being of individuals seeking treatment and continuously monitored by a licensed mental health professional (Section 3b). 3. The licensed mental health professional must inform patients of the use of AI in their treatment and provide them with the option to receive treatment from a licensed mental health professional (Section 3c). 4. The licensed mental health professional must disclose the use of AI to patients in advance and obtain their informed consent (Section 3d). 5. Any violation of the provisions of this act will result in disciplinary action by the relevant professional licensing board (Section 4a).

policy_name: Massachusetts AI in Mental Health Act
question: What are the key patient rights established by this act regarding the use of AI in their mental health treatment?
answer_1:
1. The act establishes that patients have the right to be informed of the use of AI in their mental health treatment (Section 3c).
2. Patients have the right to receive mental health services from a licensed mental health professional, without the use of AI, if they so choose (Section 3c).
3. Patients have the right to provide informed consent for the use of AI in their mental health treatment (Section 3d).

Citations:
- Section 3c: Chapter 123, Section 3c, General Laws of Massachusetts, as appearing in the 2020 Official Edition.
- Section 3d: Chapter 123, Section 3d, General Laws of Massachusetts, as appearing in the 2020 Official Edition.
answer_2: 1) Patients have the right to be informed about the use of AI in their mental health treatment. 2) Patients have the option to receive treatment from a licensed mental health professional instead of AI. 3) Patients must give informed consent before receiving mental health services through the use of AI. (Section 3, c, d of the act)

policy_name: Massachusetts AI in Mental Health Act
question: Summarize the potential penalties for a licensed mental health professional who fails to comply with the regulations outlined in this act regarding AI use.
answer_1: A licensed mental health professional who fails to comply with the regulations outlined in this act regarding AI use in providing mental health services in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts may be subject to disciplinary action by the relevant professional licensing board (Section 4(a)). The specific nature of the disciplinary action is not specified in the provided context, but it is likely to include warnings, fines, suspension, or revocation of their license, as these are common forms of disciplinary action for violations of professional standards and regulations. For more detailed information about the specific penalties and the process for disciplinary action, it is recommended to consult the relevant professional licensing board's regulations and guidelines. (Source: Chapter 123 of the General Laws, as appearing in the 2020 Official Edition)
answer_2: A licensed mental health professional who violates the provisions of this act regarding AI use in mental health services in Massachusetts will be subject to disciplinary action by the relevant professional licensing board (Section 4(a)).

policy_name: Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act
question: What are the key responsibilities and deliverables of the Task Force on Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Services Sector as outlined in the Act?
answer_1:
The Task Force on Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Services Sector, as outlined in the Act, has the following key responsibilities and deliverables:

1. Establishment (Sec. 3.a): The Task Force is established to address the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the financial services sector.

2. Membership (Sec. 3.b): The Task Force consists of representatives from various financial regulatory bodies, including the Secretary of the Treasury, the Comptroller of the Currency, the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Chairperson of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Director of the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, the Chairman of the National Credit Union Administration, and the Director of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

3. Report (Sec. 3.c): The Task Force is required to issue a report to Congress within one year of the Act's enactment. The report should contain the following:
   - A description of how banks and credit unions proactively protect themselves and consumers from fraud utilizing AI (Sec. 3.c.3.A).
   - Standard definitions for various AI terms like "generative AI", "machine learning", "natural language processing", "algorithmic AI", and "deep fakes" (Sec. 3.c.3.B).
   - A description of potential risks that could result from the use of AI by bad actors to steal consumers’ data, steal consumers’ identities, and commit fraud (Sec. 3.c.3.C).
   - A list of best practices for financial institutions to protect their customers from attempts to steal consumer data, steal consumers’ identities, or commit fraud (Sec. 3.c.3.D).
   - Legislative and regulatory recommendations for the regulation of AI and to protect consumers from data theft, identity theft, and fraud (Sec. 3.c.3.E).

4. Consultation (Sec. 3.c.2): The Task Force is required to solicit public feedback on the report and seek out and consult with industry and expert stakeholders, including depository institutions, credit unions, third-party vendors who use AI, and AI experts.

5. Termination (Sec. 3.d): The Task Force shall terminate 90 days after the final report is issued
answer_2: 1) The Task Force is established to study the use of artificial intelligence in the financial services sector. 2) It consists of members from various financial institutions and regulatory bodies, including the Secretary of the Treasury, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Chairperson of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. 3) The Task Force is required to issue a report to Congress within a year of the Act's enactment, detailing how financial institutions protect against fraud using AI, standard definitions for AI terms, potential risks, best practices, and legislative/regulatory recommendations. 4) The Task Force is also tasked with soliciting public feedback and consulting with industry and expert stakeholders in developing the report. 5) The Task Force will terminate 90 days after the final report is issued.

policy_name: Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act
question: Beyond Congress, which specific entities and individuals will receive and utilize the report generated by the Task Force, and how are they expected to use it?
answer_1:
The report generated by the Task Force on Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Services Sector will be submitted to Congress (1). Beyond Congress, the report will be of interest to various entities and individuals involved in the financial services sector, including:

1. Financial institutions: Depository institutions of varying asset sizes, credit unions of varying asset sizes, and third-party vendors who use artificial intelligence when providing services to these institutions (3b(2)(B)(i)-(iii)). These entities can use the report to understand the potential risks associated with AI, best practices for protecting customers, and legislative and regulatory recommendations for the regulation of AI.

2. Regulatory bodies: The report will be relevant to regulatory bodies such as the Secretary of the Treasury, the Comptroller of the Currency, the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Chairperson of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Director of the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, and the Chairman of the National Credit Union Administration (3b(2)). These entities can use the report to inform their regulatory policies and guidance related to AI in the financial services sector.

3. Artificial intelligence experts: The report will be of interest to AI experts who can use the information to better understand the current state of AI in the financial services sector, potential risks, and best practices for AI implementation (3b(2)(B)(iv)).

4. Legislators: The report will be useful for legislators in developing and refining legislation related to AI regulation and consumer protection in the financial services sector (3c(3)(E)).

The report is expected to be used by these entities and individuals to inform their decisions, policies, and actions related to AI in the financial services sector, with the ultimate goal of enhancing consumer protection and mitigating risks associated with AI.

Citation:
(1) Section 3(c)(1) of the Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act.
answer_2: The report generated by the Task Force will be issued to Congress (SEC. 3(c)(1)). However, the Task Force is also required to solicit public feedback on the report within 90 days of its enactment (SEC. 3(c)(2)(A)). In developing the report, the Task Force is expected to consult with industry and expert stakeholders, including depository institutions, credit unions, third-party vendors, and artificial intelligence experts (SEC. 3(c)(2)(B)). The specific use of the report by these entities and individuals is not explicitly stated in the provided context.

policy_name: Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act
question: What is the intended scope of the 'Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act' in terms of the types of financial institutions and AI technologies it covers?
answer_1:
The 'Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act' is intended to cover a variety of financial institutions, including banks, credit unions, and depository institutions of varying asset sizes, as well as credit unions of varying asset sizes (SEC. 3.b. 1-7). The Act also covers a range of AI technologies, with specific terms defined in the report issued by the Task Force, such as "generative AI", "machine learning", "natural language processing", "algorithmic AI", and "deep fakes" (SEC. 3.c.3.B). The Act focuses on the potential risks of AI being used by bad actors to steal consumer data, steal consumer identities, and commit fraud (SEC. 3.c.3.C). The report issued by the Task Force is also expected to include best practices for financial institutions to protect their customers from such attempts and legislative and regulatory recommendations for the regulation of AI to protect consumers (SEC. 3.c.3.D-E).

Citation: Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act, SEC. 3.b, SEC. 3.c.1-3, SEC. 3.c.3.B-E.
answer_2: The 'Preventing Deep Fake Scams Act' is intended to cover various financial institutions, including banks, credit unions, and depository institutions of varying asset sizes, as well as credit unions of varying asset sizes. The Act also covers a range of AI technologies, including generative AI, machine learning, natural language processing, algorithmic AI, and deep fakes. (Section 2, Findings 1, 6; Section 3, Subsection b, Membership 3-7; Section 3, Subsection c, Contents C)

policy_name: California SJR 6 ("Artificial Intelligence")
question: What specific actions does California SJR 6 urge the US President and Congress to take regarding artificial intelligence?
answer_1: California SJR 6 urges the US President and Congress to develop a comprehensive Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee and to adopt a comprehensive artificial intelligence policy. (California Legislative Counsel's Digest, SJR 6)
answer_2: California SJR 6 urges the US President and Congress to develop a comprehensive Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee and adopt a comprehensive artificial intelligence policy. This is in response to the growing impact of AI on the US workforce and economy, and the need to establish ethical standards and promote innovation. The resolution also highlights California's significant role in attracting AI investment.
